chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Al-Hasan ibn Mahboub, from Ali ibn Ri'ab, from Is'haq ibn 'Ammar, from Abu Al-Hasan (peace be upon him)

Regarding a man who performed the obligatory circumambulation (Tawaf), then became ill with an ailment that prevented him from completing the Tawaf. He (peace be upon him) said: If he had performed four circuits, he should instruct someone to perform three circuits on his behalf; thus his Tawaf is complete. And if he had performed three circuits and was unable to perform the Tawaf, then this is from what Allah has overcome him with, so there is no harm if he delays the Tawaf for one day and two days.

So if the illness leaves him, he returns and performs seven (circuits). And if his illness prolongs, he should instruct someone to perform seven (circuits) on his behalf, and he himself prays two cycles, and someone performs Sa'i on his behalf, and he has exited his Ihram. And similarly he does regarding the Sa'i and regarding the pelting of the Jamarat.

key_terms.رَمْيِ الْجِمَار: Pelting of the Jamarat (stoning of the devil)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling for a pilgrim who becomes ill and cannot complete the obligatory Tawaf?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi details the juristic distinctions for a pilgrim incapacitated during Tawaf, emphasizing the principle of *al-ghalabah* (dominance of difficulty) to relieve obligation. It establishes that while minor illness permits delaying to complete the circuits, prolonged incapacity allows for proxy performance (*tafwid*), thereby permitting the pilgrim to exit the state of Ihram, a ruling extended by scholars to Sa'i and Rami.
